p.src: Now Yuan Shao wished to have Xuande beheaded. Xuande stepped forward calmly and said, “My lord, will you heed only one side of the story and cast aside our former friendship? Since I was separated from my companions at Xuzhou, I have not known whether my second brother Yun’chang is alive or dead. There are many people in the world who resemble one another. Must every red-faced, long-bearded man be Guan? Why does my lord not investigate the matter?” Yuan Shao was a man of no settled judgment. Hearing Xuande’s words, he rebuked Ju Shou: “By wrongly listening to you, I nearly killed an innocent man.” He again invited Xuande to sit in the command tent and discussed how to avenge Yan Liang. A man below the dais promptly stepped forward and said, “Yan Liang was like a brother to me. Now that Cao the traitor has killed him, how could I fail to avenge his death?”

p.src: Xuande looked at the man. He stood eight chi tall and had a face like the mythical xiezhi; it was Wen Chou, the renowned general of Hebei. Yuan Shao was delighted. “No one but you can avenge Yan Liang. I shall give you one hundred thousand troops. Cross the Yellow River at once and pursue and destroy Cao the traitor!” Ju Shou said, “You must not. The best policy now is to maintain our encampment at Yanjin and detach troops to Guandu. If we rashly cross the river and some unforeseen change occurs, none of the army will be able to return.” Yuan Shao angrily replied, “All of you merely sap the army’s resolve with your delays, letting the days and months pass and obstructing our great enterprise! Have you never heard that in war, speed is everything?” Ju Shou withdrew and sighed: “Above, the lord is swollen with ambition; below, his followers strive only for achievement. O vast and endless Yellow River—shall I indeed cross you?” Thereafter he pleaded illness and no longer attended the councils.

p.src: Xuande said, “I have received great kindness from you, yet have had no means to repay it. I wish to accompany General Wen: first, to repay my lord’s favor, and second, to ascertain the truth about Yun’chang.” Yuan Shao was pleased and summoned Wen Chou, ordering him and Xuande to command the vanguard together. Wen Chou said, “Liu Xuande is a general repeatedly defeated; his presence would bring ill fortune to the army. Since my lord insists that he go, I shall allot him thirty thousand troops and have him form the rear division.” Thus Wen Chou set out first with seventy thousand troops, while Xuande followed with thirty thousand.

p.src: Meanwhile, after Cao Cao saw Yun’chang slay Yan Liang, his admiration for him redoubled. He submitted a memorial to the court, which enfeoffed Yun’chang as Marquis of Hanshou Village, and had a seal cast and presented to Lord Guan. Suddenly a report came that Yuan Shao had again sent his great general Wen Chou across the Yellow River and that he had already occupied the heights above Yanjin. Cao Cao first sent men to move the inhabitants to Xihe, then personally led his troops out to meet the enemy. He issued an order to the generals: the rear division was to become the van, and the van the rear; the provisions and fodder were to go first, with the soldiers following behind. Lü Qian asked, “What is the reason for placing the provisions ahead and the troops behind?” Cao Cao replied, “When provisions travel in the rear, they are often plundered, so I have ordered them placed in front.” Lü Qian said, “But what are we to do if enemy troops come upon them and seize them?” Cao Cao said, “Wait until the enemy arrives; then you will see how the matter is handled.”

p.src: Lü Qian remained doubtful and perplexed. Cao Cao ordered the provisions and baggage trains to proceed along the riverbank toward Yanjin. Cao Cao was with the rear division when he heard shouting from the front. He hastily sent someone to investigate, and the man reported: “The army of Wen Chou, the great general of Hebei, has arrived. Our troops have abandoned all the provisions and fodder and are fleeing in every direction. The rear division is still far away—what are we to do?” Pointing with his whip to two earthen mounds, Cao Cao said, “We may shelter there for a time.” Men and horses hurried toward the mounds. Cao Cao ordered all the soldiers to remove their outer garments and armor and rest awhile, and had every horse turned loose. Wen Chou’s army swept down upon them. The generals cried, “The enemy is upon us! We must gather the horses at once and retreat to Baima!” Xun You hastily stopped them, saying, “These are precisely what we can use to bait the enemy. Why retreat instead?” Cao Cao quickly glanced at Xun You and smiled. Xun You understood his intention and said no more.

p.src: After Wen Chou’s troops had seized the carts of provisions and equipment, they came to snatch the horses as well. The soldiers broke ranks and fell into disorder among themselves. Cao Cao then ordered his officers and men to charge down from the mounds together, throwing Wen Chou’s army into utter confusion. As Cao Cao’s troops closed in around him, Wen Chou stood forth and fought alone. His soldiers trampled one another, and Wen Chou could not restrain them. He had no choice but to turn his horse and flee. From atop the mound Cao Cao pointed and said, “Wen Chou is a renowned general of Hebei. Who can capture him?” Zhang Liao and Xu Huang spurred out together, shouting, “Wen Chou, do not flee!” Wen Chou looked back and saw the two generals closing on him. He steadied his iron spear, took up his bow, fitted an arrow, and shot straight at Zhang Liao. Xu Huang shouted, “Enemy general, do not loose that arrow!” Zhang Liao hastily ducked. The arrow struck his helmet and shot away its ornamental plume. Zhang Liao urged his horse onward with all his strength, but Wen Chou loosed another arrow and struck the warhorse in the cheek. The horse collapsed onto its forelegs, and Zhang Liao fell to the ground.

p.src: Wen Chou turned his horse and came back, while Xu Huang swiftly whirled his great axe and barred his way, engaging him in combat. But then Wen Chou’s troops came surging up from behind. Xu Huang judged that he could not withstand them, so he turned his horse and withdrew. Wen Chou pursued him along the river. Suddenly more than ten riders appeared, their banners fluttering. At their head a general came galloping with sword in hand. It was Guan Yun’chang, who thundered, “Enemy general, do not flee!” He met Wen Chou horse to horse. Before three bouts had passed, Wen Chou lost his nerve, turned his horse, and fled along the river. Lord Guan’s horse was swift. He overtook Wen Chou and struck him from behind with a single stroke, cutting him down from his horse. From atop the mound Cao Cao saw Lord Guan cut down Wen Chou and drove his entire force forward to slaughter the enemy. More than half the Hebei army fell into the river, and Cao Cao recovered all the provisions, fodder, and horses.

p.src: Yun’chang led a handful of riders, charging east and west through the enemy. While the slaughter was still underway, Liu Xuande arrived behind them with thirty thousand troops. Scouts ahead learned what had happened and reported to Xuande: “Once again it was the red-faced, long-bearded man who slew Wen Chou.” Xuande hastily spurred forward to see. Across the river he observed a cluster of riders sweeping back and forth like the wind, beneath a banner bearing the seven characters: “Guan Yun’chang, Marquis of Hanshou Village.” Xuande silently thanked Heaven and Earth: “So my brother truly is with Cao Cao!” He was about to call out and meet him, but the main body of Cao Cao’s army surged forward, forcing him to withdraw his troops. Yuan Shao brought up support at Guandu and established a fortified camp. Guo Tu and Shen Pei entered Yuan Shao’s presence and said, “This time again it was Guan who killed Wen Chou, yet Liu Bei falsely pretended not to know.” Yuan Shao flew into a rage and cursed, “How dare that big-eared traitor behave so!”

p.src: Before long Xuande arrived, and Yuan Shao ordered that he be dragged out and beheaded. Xuande said, “What crime have I committed?” Yuan Shao replied, “You deliberately had your brother destroy yet another of my great generals. How can you claim to be innocent?” Xuande said, “Allow me to say one thing before I die. Cao Cao has always regarded me with suspicion. Now that he knows I am with my lord, he fears that I will aid you, and so he deliberately sent Yun’chang to kill your two generals. He knew that you would surely become enraged. This is his scheme to borrow my lord’s hand to kill Liu Bei. I beg you to consider it.” Yuan Shao said, “Xuande’s words are right. You men nearly caused me to bear the disgrace of harming a worthy man.” He shouted for the attendants to withdraw and invited Xuande to take a seat in the command tent.

p.src: Xuande thanked him, saying, “I have received my lord’s magnanimous grace, yet have no way to repay it. I wish to have a trusted man carry a secret letter to Yun’chang, informing him of Liu Bei’s whereabouts. He will surely hasten here by night and day to assist my lord in destroying Cao Cao, thereby avenging Yan Liang and Wen Chou. What do you think?” Yuan Shao was overjoyed. “If I gain Yun’chang, he will be worth ten Yan Liangs and Wen Chous.” Xuande wrote the letter, but there was as yet no one to deliver it. Yuan Shao ordered the army to withdraw to Wuyang, where its linked camps stretched for scores of li, and held his troops in place without advancing. Cao Cao then ordered Xiahou Dun to lead troops in guarding the strategic pass at Guandu, while he himself marched back to Xudu and held a great banquet for all his officers to celebrate Yun’chang’s achievement. He said to Lü Qian, “The reason I formerly placed the provisions and fodder in front was to use them as bait for the enemy. Only Xun Gongda understood my intention.” All present sighed in admiration and submitted to his genius.

p.src: In the midst of the feast, a sudden report came: “The Yellow Turbans Liu Pi and Gong Du are running rampant in Runan. Cao Hong has repeatedly fought them without success and begs that troops be sent to his aid.” Hearing this, Yun’chang stepped forward and said, “I, Guan, am willing to render such service as a dog or horse and destroy the bandits of Runan.” Cao Cao said, “You have already performed a great service, Yun’chang, for which I have not yet rewarded you handsomely. How could I trouble you to campaign again?” Guan Yu said, “If I remain idle too long, I am certain to fall ill. I beg to make one more campaign.” Cao Cao admired his spirit. He mustered fifty thousand troops, appointed Yu Jin and Yue Jin as his deputies, and ordered them to depart the next day. Xun Yu privately warned Cao Cao, “Yun’chang intends to return to Liu Bei. If he learns any news of him, he will surely leave. You must not keep sending him on campaigns.” Cao Cao replied, “After he wins merit this time, I shall send him against the enemy no more.”

p.src: Now Yun’chang led his army toward Runan and encamped when he had nearly reached it. That night, two spies were seized outside the camp and brought in. Yun’chang looked at them and recognized one as Sun Qian. Guan Yu dismissed everyone nearby and asked Sun Qian, “Since our forces were scattered, I have heard nothing of your whereabouts. What brings you here now?” Sun Qian replied, “After fleeing the disaster, I wandered as far as Runan and was fortunate enough to be taken in by Liu Pi. But why are you now with Cao Cao, General? And I wonder whether Ladies Gan and Mi are safe and well?”

p.src: Guan Yu then related the whole course of events in detail. Sun Qian said, “I recently heard that Lord Xuande is with Yuan Shao. I wished to go and join him, but had no opportunity. Liu Pi and Gong Du have now submitted to Yuan Shao and are helping him attack Cao Cao. Fortunately, you have come here, General. They therefore specially sent a soldier to guide me and ordered me to pose as a spy so that I might bring you word. Tomorrow they will feign defeat in battle. You should quickly escort the two ladies to Yuan Shao and reunite with Lord Xuande.” Guan Yu said, “Since my brother is with Yuan Shao, I must hasten there day and night. I only regret that I slew two of Yuan Shao’s generals; I fear this may now cause trouble.” Sun Qian said, “I shall go first to discover the true state of affairs there, then return and report to you.” Guan Yu said, “If I can but see my elder brother once, I will not shrink even from ten thousand deaths. When I return to Xuchang this time, I shall take leave of Cao Cao at once.” That very night, he secretly sent Sun Qian away.

p.src: The next day, Guan Yu led his troops out, and Gong Du came forth fully armed to meet him. Guan Yu cried, “Why have you rebelled against the imperial court?” Gong Du replied, “You are one who has betrayed his lord. How dare you accuse me?” Guan Yu said, “How have I betrayed my lord?” Gong Du said, “Liu Xuande is with Yuan Benchu, yet you follow Cao Cao. Why is that?” Guan Yu said no more, but spurred his horse and rode forward, brandishing his blade. Gong Du fled, and Guan Yu pursued him. Gong Du turned and called to Guan Yu, “The kindness of one’s former lord must never be forgotten. Press forward swiftly, my lord, and I shall yield Runan to you.” Guan Yu understood and drove his troops forward in a fierce assault. Liu Pi and Gong Du pretended to lose and feigned a rout, scattering in all directions. Yun’chang took the commandery and counties, restored order among the people, and led his army back to Xuchang. Cao Cao went beyond the city walls to welcome him and rewarded the soldiers for their service.

p.src: After the feast, Yun’chang returned home and paid his respects to his two sisters-in-law outside their door. Lady Gan asked, “You have now campaigned twice, brother. Have you learned any news of the Imperial Uncle?” Guan Yu replied, “Not yet.” After Guan Yu withdrew, the two ladies wept bitterly behind the door, saying, “The Imperial Uncle must be dead! Our second brother fears that we sisters will grieve, and so he conceals it and will not tell us.”

p.src: As they wept, an old soldier who had accompanied the campaign heard their ceaseless crying and called from outside the door, “My ladies, do not weep. Our lord is alive and presently with Yuan Shao in Hebei.” The lady asked, “How do you know this?” The soldier replied, “I followed General Guan on campaign, and someone spoke of it on the battlefield.” The lady urgently summoned Yun’chang and rebuked him: “The Imperial Uncle has never failed you. Yet now, having received Cao Cao’s favor, you have utterly forgotten your former loyalty. Why did you not tell me the truth?” Guan Yu bowed his head to the ground and said, “My brother truly is in Hebei now; I did not dare let you know because I feared the news might leak out. The matter must be planned deliberately; we must not act in haste.” Lady Gan said, “You must make haste, brother.” Guan Yu withdrew and pondered how to leave, unable to sit or stand at ease.

As Guan Yu sat brooding, Zhang Liao entered and congratulated him: “I hear you learned news of Xuande on the battlefield, brother, so I have come especially to offer my congratulations.” Guan Yu replied, “Though my former lord is alive, I have not yet been able to see him. What cause is there for joy?” Zhang Liao asked, “How does your bond with Xuande compare to the bond between you and me?” Guan Yu replied, “You and I are joined in friendship; but Xuande and I are friends and brothers, brothers and also lord and subject. How could the two be discussed in the same terms?” Zhang Liao asked, “Now that Xuande is in Hebei, will you go and join him?” Guan Yu replied, “How could I ever betray the words I gave before? Wenyuan, you must convey my respects and intentions to the Chancellor.” Zhang Liao returned and reported Guan Yu’s words to Cao Cao. Cao Cao said, “I have a plan of my own to keep him here.”

p.src: Chen Zhen received the letter and departed. Guan Yu went inside and informed his two sisters-in-law, then immediately proceeded to the Chancellor’s residence to take leave of Cao Cao. Cao Cao knew why he had come and hung a sign at the gate announcing that he would receive no visitors. Guan Yu returned in dejection and ordered the attendants who had formerly followed him to prepare the carts and horses and stand ready day and night; he instructed everyone in the household that every object bestowed upon him must be left behind and not so much as a fraction carried away. The next day, he again went to the Chancellor’s residence to offer thanks and take his leave, but the sign refusing visitors once more hung at the gate. p.src: When he had finished writing, he sealed the letter securely and sent a man to deliver it to the Chancellor’s residence; meanwhile, he sealed up every piece of gold and silver he had received and placed it in the treasury, hung the seal of Marquis of Hanshou Village in the hall, and invited the two ladies into their carriage. Guan Yu mounted Red Hare, took the Green Dragon blade in hand, and, leading his former attendants as they escorted the carriage, made straight for the northern gate. The gate officers barred his way. Guan Yu glared, leveled his blade, and gave a mighty shout; all the gate officers fell back. Once through the gate, Guan Yu told his followers, “Escort the carriage and go on ahead. If anyone pursues us, I shall deal with them myself. You must not alarm the two ladies.” The attendants pushed the carriage onward and set out along the highway.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Cao was still deliberating the matter of Lord Guan when his attendants reported that a letter had arrived from him. As soon as Cao Cao finished reading it, he exclaimed in alarm, “Yunzhang has gone!” Just then, the commander guarding the north gate hurried in to report: “Lord Guan forced his way through the gate and departed. With more than twenty attendants, carriages, equipment, saddles, and horses, he has headed north.” Another man came from Lord Guan’s residence and reported: “Lord Guan sealed up all the gold, silver, and other gifts he had received. The ten beautiful women have been left in separate inner chambers. His seal as Marquis of Hanshou Village hangs in the main hall. He took none of the servants assigned to him by the Prime Minister, but departed through the north gate with only his original followers and his personal baggage.” Everyone was dumbfounded. One general stepped forward and declared, “Give me three thousand armored horsemen, and I shall capture Guan alive and deliver him to the Prime Minister!” All looked and saw that it was General Cai Yang.
